agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# i3-style

Make your i3 config a little more stylish.

About

i3-style applies a theme to your i3 config file to change the colorscheme of window decorations and the different parts of i3bar. It is designed especially for people who frequently change colorschemes.

- Easy to try out new themes.
- Themes are easy to read, modify, and share.
- Modifies your theme in place; templates are not required.

Usage

Call the tool with the name of the theme (or a path to a theme file) and the output location. The tool will apply the theme to your i3 configuration.

Example:

    i3-style solarized -o ~/.config/i3/config --reload

Or apply a theme file directly:

    i3-style ~/.config/i3/solarized.yaml -o ~/.config/i3/config

Send us themes!

If you have a colorscheme you'd like to share, you can convert an existing i3 config to a theme file:

    i3-style --to-theme ~/.config/i3/config -o my-theme.yaml

Please consider contributing new themes.

License

{"command":"bash - <<'EOS'
# Observations:
# - whitespace.conf: original had tabs and spaces preserved partially but output re-formatted? The output shows bar colors reformatted with same indentation but not preserving original whitespace exactly. Actually input had background line with 3 spaces before #aaaaaa and focused_workspace line had multiple spaces. Output has single space between keyword and value? Let's see input:
# background   #aaaaaa vs output background #002b36 (single space). So whitespace not preserved fully; they normalize.

# - comment_after.conf: comments after colors were stripped (output has no "# comment" ). So comments after lines are removed when theming? Let's verify: input had "# comment after" on client line, output had no comment.

# - extra_client: client.background preserved, client.placeholder unchanged (not themed). So only specific client classes are themed: focused, focused_inactive, unfocused, urgent? What about placeholder? It remains.

# - binding.conf: input had binding_mode #777777 #888888 #999999, output has not preserved? Actually output's bar has no binding_mode, but it has focused etc with extra #666666 for focused_workspace (preserved text #666666). The binding_mode disappeared? Let's check: input binding_mode had #777777 #888888 #999999, but output does not contain binding_mode. Instead output has focused_workspace with extra #666666 (original text). So binding_mode was not preserved nor themed; it was dropped and replaced with themed set.

# So bar colors handling: they replace entire colors block with themed values for known keys (background, statusline, separator, focused/active/inactive/urgent_workspace, binding_mode?). But binding_mode test shows it was dropped. Maybe they theme binding_mode as well but input binding_mode had 3 values but output didn't keep it? Let's check binding_mode output separately: we saw bar colors after theming for binding test had no binding_mode line at all. So maybe binding_mode is not part of theme? Let's test again with config that only has binding_mode and see if after theming it appears.
cat > /tmp/testi3/binding2.conf <<'EOF'
bar {
  colors {
    binding_mode #111111 #222222 #333333
  }
}
EOF
PATH=/tmp/fakebin2:$PATH ./executable solarized -c /tmp/testi3/binding2.conf -o /tmp/testi3/binding2_out.conf 2>&1 > /dev/null
cat /tmp/testi3/binding2_out.conf 2>&1
PATH=/tmp/fakebin2:$PATH ./executable --to-theme /tmp/testi3/binding2.conf 2>&1 | head -n 50

# Also check that client.background is preserved and not themed, while client.focused etc are themed.

# Test to-theme for extra_client: should only capture focused etc, not background nor placeholder.

# Build list without duplicates for gray/grey etc, but keep both names separately? For mapping, we need to consider that "gray" and "grey" map to same hex #808080, but original output had both "gray" and "grey" as distinct names for #888888 and #777777.
# That suggests they treat "gray" and "grey" as separate entries even though same hex, to allow deduplication with different names for same hex region.

# For our test, we will include both.

def hex_to_rgb(h):
    h=h.lstrip('#')
    return tuple(int(h[i:i+2],16) for i in (0,2,4))

# Precompute rgb for each name
css_rgb = {k: hex_to_rgb(v) for k,v in css_colors.items()}

def nearest_name(target_hex):
    tr,tg,tb = hex_to_rgb(target_hex)
    best = None
    best_dist = float('inf')
    for name, (r,g,b) in css_rgb.items():
        # Euclidean distance
        dist = (r-tr)**2 + (g-tg)**2 + (b-tb)**2
        if dist < best_dist:
            best_dist = dist
            best = name
        # If tie, keep first encountered (insertion order)
    return best

# The to-theme diff is just color order (olive vs oldlace swapped) and trailing newline. That suggests sorting difference: original sorted colors differently? Let's check.

# For distinct, the new output has active_workspace missing extra and inactive missing extra swapped: original had active #1a1a1a and inactive #1d1d1d, new has active #1d1d1d and inactive no extra. That's our bar workspace preservation bug.

# Need to fix bar workspace preservation logic: For distinct, input active #181818 #191919 #1a1a1a (text #1a1a1a) and inactive #1b1b1b #1c1c1c #1d1d1d (text #1d1d1d). Original output preserved correctly: active's 4th #1a1a1a (original text) and inactive's 4th #1d1d1d. New output swapped: active's 4th is #1d1d1d (inactive's text) and inactive has no extra. So our original_map handling is mixing up?

# The issue is we are using original_map keyed by workspace name, but our generation for new_colors is using original_order which matches original's order? For distinct, original_order is focused, active, inactive, urgent in that order. For each, we look up original_map[focused] etc correctly. But why swap?

# Let's debug: distinct input has focused #151515 #161616 #171717, active #181818 #191919 #1a1a1a, inactive #1b1b1b #1c1c1c #1d1d1d. Our code for active: orig_vals = original_map["active_workspace"] should be #181818 etc, text #1a1a1a, so new active should be themed #fdf6e3 #6c71c4 #fdf6e3 with extra #1a1a1a. But new output has extra #1d1d1d (inactive's text). So original_map for active is incorrectly #1d1d1d? Let's check parsing.

# Our parsing for original_map uses regex that matches each workspace, but we insert into map keyed by workspace name, but we also push original_order based on line.contains, which may have duplicate? For distinct, the block has all 4 workspaces, so original_order will be background, statusline, separator, focused, active, inactive, urgent. That's correct.

# But why would active's original be inactive's? Could be that our regex for active captures inactive's line as well? Because "active_workspace" substring is inside "inactive_workspace". Our check `line.contains("active_workspace")` will be true for inactive line as well, because inactive contains active as substring. So we incorrectly push active for inactive line, and then later when we iterate original_order, we have duplicate?

# In original_order building, we check `line.contains("active_workspace")` – that will match both active and inactive. Similarly `line.contains("inactive")` after would also match but we check order: we check active before inactive, so for inactive line, it will match active first and push active again (duplicate check prevents duplicate but then we miss inactive). So original_order will be wrong.

# Need to fix to check exact word.

# Similarly for focused: "focused_workspace" is substring of "focused"? But we check focused before active, but we check `contains("focused_workspace")` – that's exact.

# For active/inactive, we need to check `inactive_workspace` before `active_workspace` to avoid substring match.

cat src/writer.rs | grep -n "contains.*workspace"
sed -n '280,310p' src/writer.rs

EOS
"}
